wraitii opened PR #15205 from wraitii:fix/egraph-cloned-remat to bytecodealliance:main:

Egraph elaboration can clone instructions when placing them in separate dominance scopes, including when LICM hoists constants. These clones receive new value IDs that the rematerialization set does not recognize, potentially extending live ranges and increasing register pressure.

Check rematerialization eligibility through the existing value_to_best_value mapping so clones retain the original value’s eligibility.

Add regression coverage for a cloned constant hoisted out of a loop and a cloned non-constant instruction without loops. Both cases fail before the fix.

Validation: 82 egraph test files and 216 codegen unit tests pass.

PR written by GPT 6.1 sol following investigation by Opus 5.5 . Leads to obvious incorrect spilling of constants in a JS JIT I'm working on. As with my earlier PRs, I've spot-checked that the diff looks correct for what the AIs report the problem is, but I cannot really confirm that this is the minimal or cleanest fix, feel free to pong back.

wraitii commented on PR #15205:

Ran Sightglass, Apple Silicon M1 max: 29 workloads, 20 samples per engine.

  • Compilation: 4.3% less time overall.
  • Execution: +0.2%, no statistically significant overall change.

A 50-sample follow-up confirmed:

Workload Change Codex explanation
shootout-switch compilation −68.8% time large switch with constants, this was hitting a worst-case in regalloc
TinyGo regex execution −2.8%
heapsort execution −1.8%
libsodium-hash3 execution +3.7% more instructions in the inner loop (in printf, it seems)
hex-simd execution +4.8% more instructions in the inner loop (in the vector loop)

Those results read decently odd to me to be honest - i would have expected more functions with concrete wins, and the regressions might highlight unrelated issues. The compile-time win in shootout switch is pretty clear though.

kdf_hkdf +3.0%
auth +2.9%
hash +2.6%

After some digging, it seems the culprit is that these now rematerialize constant-operand ALU operations, like "val & 255" & the like, when this seems un-necessary, as the original constants can stay in registers across the loop. This feels like it should be decided at the register-level, or cleaned-up afterwards.
Unfortunately seems like a decently real regression in some cases then. Could be limited to actual constants, where it's less likely to perform poorly.

cfallin commented on PR #15205:

Thanks! The change itself does-what-it-says-on-the-tin, and looks correct to me. I'm somewhat confused by the ad-hoc benchmark result presentation here though -- would you mind running the full suite, and showing effects on compile time and run-time separately?

wraitii commented on PR #15205:

Ran the default suite with default settings (took ~15 minutes on my machine):
fullsuite-res.txt

The difference _mostly_ seems to come down to constant-op ALU operations that get un-necessarily rematerialized inside loops when their results can be held in register across the loop.
